column2: the cards model the ISVR rig, not a player: Davies, Pinho and English blew the whistle from a regulated, metered air supply in a 20 C anechoic room, so dry air at 20 C is the cited state of every card, and the blowing pressures are computed from the measured flows and are not re-derived. A played whistle carries exhaled breath. The shared woodwind pack breath-woodwind-exhaled-coltman1966-nederveen1969 (27 C, 101325 Pa, saturated, 4.5 percent dry CO2 and 16.5 percent dry O2; Coltman, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 40(1), 1966, p. 101; Nederveen, Acoustical Aspects of Woodwind Instruments, 1969, sec. 12 p. 28; Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, sec. 8.1 p. 191) has a sound speed of 345.36 m/s against 343.2 m/s for dry 20 C air, which would raise every note by about 11 cents (measured on the five pan-pipe cards, which do carry it: 10.9 to 11.0 cents), and a density of 1.1815 against 1.2041 kg/m3, which would raise the jet speed at a fixed blowing pressure by about 1 percent. The pack is the generic woodwind breath state (the top of its own CO2 bracket), not a measurement of a played whistle. The nearest measured bore is a played flute: Coltman, Physics Today 21(11), 1968, p. 27, found about 2.5 percent CO2 and 25.8 to 26.5 C in a 21 C room, about 5.7 cents above the pack by an ideal-gas sum (SunnySnow, Agent Mail 9244), so a played whistle would sit about 11 to 17 cents above the dry-air cards. No bore temperature or composition of a played tin whistle is in the library
column3: temperature 288.15 to 310.15 K, the pack's declared validity range; dry CO2 2.5 to 4.5 percent, its published breath-cycle bracket
column5: absolute pitch of a played whistle against a recording of one (about 11 to 17 cents) and the jet speed at a given blowing pressure (about 1 percent)
column6: a measured bore temperature and CO2 fraction of a played tin whistle, and the blowing pressure or flow of a played note

column2: the jet gain g of the Nolle/Price transfer in the PLAYING condition (pipe flow open, jet struck at its centre): Price et al. 2015 fitted 0.145 with the pipe flow blocked (0.20 with a small pipe flow), their model derivation assumes 1 for an unblocked jet, and they could not measure it; no value is tried here

column2: height of the wedge tip above the bore, inside the 2.4 mm wall: the paper gives the wedge angle (about 25 degrees) and its 11 mm upper surface but not where the tip sits, and 11 mm at 25 degrees rises 4.6 mm, more than the wall, so the wedge is not a ramp from the tip to the outer surface of the tube. The recipe renders both ends of a stated bracket and prefers neither: a tip 0.5 mm above the bore with the 25 degree face rising from it, and a face straight through the wall
column3: [0.0005, 0.0024] m above the bore (0.0024: the face rises straight through the wall)

column6: a section drawing or photograph of the mouthpiece

column2: the blowing pressure reaches the voice as a staircase at the cards' control rate, 1000 Hz: fs-scenario samples the gesture once per control tick and the voice holds that value until the next. A 50 ms onset ramp arrives as 50 steps, the first jumping from 0 to 1/50 of the target pressure, and the 10.5 ms release as about 10, the last dropping to 0. A finer rate is refused (MagentaBadger, Agent Mail 8043: 2000 and 4000 Hz on recorder a1 and whistle D5, 48000 Hz on recorder f1 and a1, whistle D5 and G5 and flute G4): a smooth ramp passes through pressures of a fraction of a Pa, where the jet is slower than its convection history allows, and the voice refuses rather than run outside its domain. A real breath passes those pressures in a few milliseconds; below some speed there is a slow viscous flow and no convected jet. The cards stay at 1000 Hz until the jet has a stated state below its lowest valid speed
column5: onset and release claims: speaking time, the attack transient and any line at 1 kHz; no finer rate renders, so the staircase's own effect on the attack cannot be A/B tested
column6: a jet with a stated state below its lowest valid speed (no jet below a stated threshold speed, or a convection history sized for the slowest jet the gesture reaches); then the cards move to a fine control rate with their controls budget raised

column2: development of the flow along the windway: both windway laws take a fully developed planar channel, the cards' `windway slit` (quasi-steady, 12 mu L U/h^2 + rho U^2/2 with a uniform exit head) and the verified but unvalidated `windway unsteady` (its CONTRACT scope excludes entrance development). With the cards' gas (dry air at 293.15 K, rho 1.2041 kg/m3, mu 1.8134e-5 Pa s), h 1.48 mm and L 24.55 mm, the parallel-plate development length L_e = 0.011 D_h Re_Dh (D_h = 2h) is 2.3 L at D5 (67 Pa, slit bulk speed 8.73 m/s, Re_h 858), 3.0 L at G5 (108 Pa), 4.4 L at D6 (210 Pa), 6.6 L at A6c (444 Pa) and 8.7 L at D7c (758 Pa, 33.5 m/s, Re_h 3292); L/U runs from 2.8 ms at D5 to 0.73 ms at D7c. THE HELD NOTE IS OUTSIDE BOTH LAWS on every whistle card: the flow never develops, so an inviscid core reaches the exit with wall layers of order sqrt(nu L/U) = 0.11 to 0.21 mm against the 0.74 mm half-gap. Along that core Bernoulli sets the exit centre speed sqrt(2 dp/rho): 10.6 m/s at D5 and 35.5 m/s at D7c, where the slit law gives a bulk speed of 8.7 and 33.5 m/s and a Poiseuille centre speed of 13.1 and 50.3 m/s. During the attack, for about L/U after a pressure change, each station sees an impulsively started channel, which `windway unsteady` carries and `slit` omits. Numbers: HazyDune, Agent Mail 8349 and 8373, recomputed per card on 2026-10-28 (8349's D5 row used the breath gas; the whistle cards use dry air)
column5: every held-note jet speed and exit profile on every whistle card (the jet's speed, transit and Reynolds number follow the slit law's bulk speed); the attack's one-dimensional treatment holds only for about L/U after each pressure change
column6: a developing-flow (boundary-layer) windway model, bead pexfp.135.4 (waits for a ruling); grading data in bead pexfp.135.3 (no open direct measurement of a whistle windway found; Ségoufin's 2000 thesis Fig. 5.13 measures a recorder's exit profile)
